titleFa: کتاب The Return of the Native
author: Thomas Hardy
introFa: کتاب «The Return of the Native» نوشته Thomas Hardy یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Return of the Native»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: NARRATING THE NATIVE 149 observer. In so doing it seems to affirm the ideology of Victorian anthropology. Yet the anthropologically informed analyses of the customs and superstitions of the na- tive heathfolk both subscribe to and contest tenets of contemporary anthropologi- cal thought. Furthermore, the native heath-dwellers themselves are ambiguously esteemed in the novel. They embody values that the novel seems to endorse, but they are also represented in ethnographic formulations of high and low stages of culture. Their voices are represented in dialogue that appears mimetic but is often orchestrated to illustrate the limitations of their primitive ways of comprehending their world. Victorian ambivalence about die relationship between die primitive past and die civilized present, and about die supposedly "great advantages of civili- sation" (Lubbock 50), lies behind this narrative dissonance, a dissonance that I read dirough nineteenth-century evolutionary theories of the intellectual progress of die race, and die stories diey told to explain die disappearance, die survival, and die return of "die native."5 Preoccupied witii evolutionary time and die connections between die "primitive" heatii and its "enemy," "civilization" (56), The Return of the Native opens witii several stunning personifications diat return to a primitive way of knowing—to a stage of human culture when man projected an image of himself onto inscrutable, natural phenomena. These personifications mydiologize die land diat "when otiier tilings sank brooding to sleep ... appeared slowly to awake and listen" (54). The anima- tion of die headi in the prologue to die narrative action situates die reader at mul- tiple beginnings—of die headi before die appearance of humanity, of die narrative tale of "diree women," and of human knowledge. Like early man, who be- lieved in die "idea of pervading life and will in nature" (Tylor 1: 287), die narra- tive consciousness endows die "titanic" (54) land mass widi moods, and natural phenomena widi volition: "The face of the headi by its mere complexion added half an hour to evening: it could in like manner retard die dawn, sadden noon, an- ticipate die frowning of storms scarcely generated" (53). "The sombre stretch of rounds and hollows" of Egdon "seemed to rise and.meet die evening gloom in pure sympatiiy, die headi exhaling darkness as rapidly as die heavens precipitated it" (54). The narration here revisits an earlier state of consciousness—a nonem- pirical, subjective way of knowing diat appears to be valued for its epistemological and representational "trutii." These personifications are prefaced by die claim diat die headi "could best be felt when it could not clearly be seen, its complete effect and explanation lying in dlis and die succeeding hours before die next dawn; dien, and only tiien, did it tell its true tale" (53, my emphases). In dlis mode of percep- tion, "effect and explanation"—emotion and intellection—are integrated. The "trudi" of die tale is narratable not as topographical description of visible features, but as personification—die perceptive and expressive mode of die primitive con- sciousness.6 The opening personifications of die heatii grant epistemological and represen- tational authority to primitive, animistic vision, and they acknowledge die subjec- Downloaded by [Columbia University] at 12:49 14 November 2014

150 PATRICIA O'HARA tivity of that vision. The darkness essential to comprehending the "true tale" bodies forth indeterminate semblances and endless possibilities that the mind's eye—the subjective imagination—reconstitutes according to its "moods." "Nobody," the nar- rator declares, "could be said to understand the heath who had not been there at [this transition point of its nightly roll into darkness] " (53). Only in the darkness— of night, of the past, and of the mind—can the truth of the tale be revealed: "During winter darkness, tempests, and mists," the heath "was aroused to reciprocity, for the storm was its lover, and the wind its friend. Then it became the home of strange phantoms; and it was found to be the hitherto unrecognized original of those wild regions of obscurity which are vaguely felt to be compassing us about in midnight dreams of flight and disaster, and are never thought of after the dream till revived by scenes like this" (54) .7 From the nightmare realm of the subconscious, the intel- lectually advanced narrative consciousness retrieves visions of "strange phantoms" that anthropologists attributed to primitive man, superstitious peasants, and chil- dren, children like Johnny Nunsuch: "Only unusual sights frightened [Johnny Nunsuch].... The thorn-bushes which arose in his path from time to time... whis- tled gloomily, and had a ghastly habit after dark of putting on the shapes of jump- ing madmen, sprawling giants, and hideous cripples" (125). The narrator's personification of die sleeping giant, Egdon Heath, exhumes those visions of child- hood in an effort to regenerate a lost imaginative vitality. Nineteenth-century social evolutionary thought, however, cast doubts on the au- thenticity of this sort of literary return to an earlier mental stage. Anthropologists like Tylor, who traced the development of mind and consciousness from primitive animism to modern empiricism, insisted upon an essential difference between the ancient mydimaker, who believed in the reality of his personification, and the mod- ern writer, whose analogies "are but fancies": "[Men of past ages] heard the voices of the hill-dwarfs answering in the echo, and the chariot of the Heaven-god rat- ding in thunder over the solid firmament.... [W]hat we call poetry was to them real life, not as to the modern versemaker a masquerade of gods and heroes" (1: 297). From the perspective of the science of culture, the modern writer's use of per- sonification is nothing more than a "masquerade," or an inauthentic, merely literary, gesture—a supposition with troubling implications for the post-Romantic enter- prise of poetry and fiction. As early as the 1830s Tennyson voiced an anxiety diat would resonate as the century wore on: Why take the style of those heroic times? For nature brings not back the Mastodon, Nor we those times; and why should any man Remodel models? (The Epic" lines 35-38) While Tennyson was able to allay his doubts and remodel die medieval Arthuriad into the twelve books of the Idylls of the King, later Victorians' efforts to resuscitate lit- erary "mastodons" are haunted by an acute awareness of the "long line of disillusive centuries" (Return 225) diat severed the past from die present Downloaded by [Columbia University] at 12:49 14 November 2014

NARRATING THE NATIVE 151 Throughout the nineteenth century, writers worried that the spirit of rational in- quiry was destructive to the free play of the imagination. However, where writers earlier in the century kept faith in the value of an imaginative return to the world's youth, the Victorians' faith in the wisdom of ancient mythic literatures was eroded by ethnographic and anthropological representations of the moral and intellectual condition of primitive tribes. Writing in 1825 of the "incompatible advantages of... the clear discernment of truth and the exquisite enjoyment of fiction" (376), Macaulay observed that "as civilization advances, poetry almost necessarily de- clines" (372). Macaulay's argument about the decline of poetry takes a bénéficient view of the "rude state of society" in which "men are children with a greater variety of ideas" (375) : "He who, in an enlightened and literary society, aspires to be a great poet, must first become a little child. He must take to pieces the whole web of his mind. He must unlearn much of that knowledge which has perhaps constituted hitherto his chief title to superiority" (376). As an antidote to enlightenment, Macaulay here prescribes a dismantling of the civilized mind—an act of willed in- tellectual oblivion. Shelley based his "defence" of the noble, mythopoeic offices of the poet on a version of the "youth of the world" as a pristine state of consciousness when "language is vitally metaphorical; that is, it marks the before unapprehended relations of things, and perpetuates their apprehension" (481-82). And Wordsworth could proclaim that he would "rather be / A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn" (lines 9-10) precisely because he trusted in the imaginative superiority of the visionary glimpses available to the pagan mythmakers.8 In an 1890 journal entry, Thomas Hardy made the following relevant comment about the imagination and levels of culture: Dec. 18. Mr. E. Clodd this morning gives an excellently neat answer to my question why the superstitions of a remote Asiatic and a Dorset labourer are the same;—'The attitude of man,' he says, 'at correspond- ing levels of culture, before like phenomena, is pretty much the same, your Dorset peasant representing the persistence of the barbaric idea which confuses persons and things, and founds wide generalizations on the slenderest analogies.' (This 'barbaric idea which confuses persons and things' is, by the way, also common to the highest imaginative genius—that of the poet.) (The Life and Work of Thomas Hardy 241) This journal entry has been cited in discussions of Hardy's responses to the up- heavals produced by nineteenth-century evolutionary sciences and as evidence of Hardy's recognition and approval of the affinities between "lower" states of culture and the highest artistic state, the creative imagination.9 For instance, J. B. Bullen ar- gues that the Clodd passage illustrates Hardy's recognition of the affinities between the savage mind and the artistic sensibility, and that those affinities were acknowl- edged by Tylor and Max Mûller (184). I maintain, however, that writers like Tylor and Mûller worked toward deprivileging those affinities. Furthermore, I find it highly peculiar that Hardy professed (in an 1890 journal entry that he later selected to include in the autobiography) to have found an "excellently neat" answer in the form of social evolutionary theory and the concept of cultural survivals, when it is abundantly clear from reading The Return of the Native that he was cognizant of that Downloaded by [Columbia University] at 12:49 14 November 2014

152 PATRICIA O'HARA "answer" in the 1870s, the decade in which Clodd himself published his popular- ization of social evolution, The Childhood of the World (1878). Whether or not Clodd's answer settled the question for Hardy in 1890 (and unlike odiers who have com- mented on die journal entry, I remain unconvinced that it did), the 1870s found him troubled and uncertain about how to negotiate a relationship between primi- tive habits of mind diat survived from the "childhood of the world" and the mod- ern literary imagination. Indeed, the "childhood of the world" metaphor for mankind's cultural prehis- tory remained the dominant one throughout the century, but social evolutionary science radically shifted the connotative tenor of die trope. Drawing upon die evo- lutionary formula that ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny, social evolutionists re- peatedly asserted diat the intellectual progress of die race was re-enacted in the intellectual growdi of each civilized individual, who had only to remember his own childhood fancies if he wished to understand primitive man's belief in the actuality of phantasmal beings. However, ethnographic and anthropological analyses of die barbarity of primitive rituals and of the naivete of mydiological personifications of nature called into question die desirability of a return to die youthful state of die imagination and the "spirit which looks on all objects in nature as animate" (Comte 68). Reversing die eighteendi-century idealization of die Noble Savage and die Romantic apodieosis of the visionary states of childhood, social evolutionists read civilized man's outgrowing of childhood phantoms as a positive, beneficial sign of his affiliation widi a mature, civilized culture. As die colonialist-narrator of Robert Louis Stevenson's 1892 story, "The Beach of Falesa," says of die easily beguiled na- tives of die Soudi Sea island he inhabits, "It's easy to find out what Kanakas diink. Just go back to yourself anyway round from ten to fifteen years old, and diere's an average Kanaka" (153). While tiiose who wrote about die progress of die intellect from primitive mydiology to civilized empiricism betrayed ambivalence about contemporary man's "blunted mythologie sense" (Tylor 1: 303), diey nonedieless expressed a dis- trust of die figurative and die fictive diat is characteristic of nineteendi-century scientific diought.10 Widi its commitment to a seemingly empiricist mediodology, cultural evolutionary dieory's teleological vision of civilization regarded metaphor- ical constructions as misapprehension.11 The comparative mythographer and philologist F. Max Mûller, for example, dieorized about die development of mydi "in die historical progress of die human mind" (104), and his hypodiesis diat mydiology represented a "disease of language" offers a striking contrast to an ear- lier nineteenth-century valorization of die primitive imagination and die vitality of mydi and metaphor. Mûller proposed diat mydiological narratives could be etymo- logically traced back to word roots—diat mydiological narratives had arisen out of metaphors diat were "infections" (106), or linguistic shifts away from original ety- mological designations. The "disease of language" dieory was widely circulated and debated and ultimately refuted by Andrew Lang and Tylor.12 Yet Tylor and Mûller did share an antipadiy to figurative language as a tool for die formulation and Downloaded by [Columbia University] at 12:49 14 November 2014

NARRATING THE NATIVE 153 expression of thought. Mûller's opening comments in the "Philosophy of Mythology" essay attempt to heighten awareness of the "mythological infections" (104) that pervade supposedly rational contemporary discourse. "We are not so ready," he warns, "to see that it is our fate, too, to move in allegories which illustrate things intellectual by visions exhibited to the fancy" (104). For Tylor metaphor and analogy impeded civilized, rational inquiry and the expression of "things intellec- tual": "[H]alf the vast defect of thought as determined by the influence of lan- guage" is "due to the fact that speech is a scheme worked out by the rough and ready application of material metaphor and imperfect analogy, in ways fitting rather the barbaric education than our own" (2: 446). However, the influential French philosopher Auguste Comte read quite differ- ently the relationship between primitive and civilized modes of knowledge, and Comte's reconciliation of the "fetichistic spirit" (his phrase for what British evolu- tionism termed "animism") and modern positivist inquiry is relevant to the figura- tive strategies of The Return of the Native.13 Comte's Positive Philosophy held enormous appeal for Victorian intellectuals like George Eliot, George Henry Lewes, Harriet Martineau, and John Stuart Mill because it systematically reconstructed the history of mind and knowledge to incorporate earlier ways of knowing and feeling into a new, and synthetic, positive knowledge. Comte's "luminous classification of the sci- ences" (Lewes 652) held that all forms of knowledge pass through three successive stages: the theological (causes attributed to supernatural agents), the metaphysical (causes attributed to invisible forces), and the positive (causes attributed to scientif- ically verifiable conditions and laws). In volume 3 (SocialDynamics) of the System of Positivé Polity, Comte identified fetichism as the initial stage of theologism (theolo- gism being the most unnatural and erroneous form of explanation of causes), but he maintained that "contrary to the prevailing prejudice" the "Fetichistic spirit... is superior" to the Theological spirit in "spontaneity" and "truth" (68). Its value as a method of inquiry lay in its "consecration]" of "concrete observation" (77), its fos- tering of man's sympathy and sense of harmony with all nature, and its simplicity and naturalness. Given die impossibility of acquiring Absolute Knowledge, Comte rea- soned, man will always enact a "Fictitious Syndiesis" of earlier forms of knowledge with positive, empirically verifiable ones.14 In The Return of the Native, a remarkable description of the "infinitesimal veg- etable causes" of the auditory effect of the wind works toward homologizing the primitive "fetichistic mood" with "one of more advanced quality"; and it is indebted to Comte's accreditation of primitive modes of thought It was a worn whisper, dry and papery, and it brushed so distinctly across the ear It was the united products of infinitesimal vegetable causes, and these were neither stems, leaves, fruits, blades, prickles, lichen, nor moss. They were the mummied heath-bells of the past summer.... [S] o low was an individual sound from these a combination of hundreds only just emerged from silence.... One inwardly saw the infinity of those combined multitudes; and perceived that each of the tiny trumpets was seized on, entered, scoured and emerged from by the wind as thoroughly as if it were as vast as a crater. 154 PATRICIA O'HARA "The spirit moved them." A meaning of the phrase forced itself upon the attention; and an emotional listener's fetichistic mood might have ended in one of more advanced quality. It was not, after all, that the left-hand expanse of old blooms spoke, or the right hand, or those of the slope in front; but it was the single person of something else speaking through each at once. (105-06) In its representation of an individual act of observation, the passage reinvents the intellectual progress of the race, with the typographically highlighted declaration— " 'The spirit moved them' "—signalling a merger of emotion and reason. By repre- senting the "inward" subjectivity of perception as continuous with more empirically accurate observation of effects, Hardy portrays the source of knowledge as neither merely naive animation of nature nor purely scientific formulation of atmospheric and "vegetable" conditions. The culminating statement that a "single person of something else" spoke through the blooms confesses its inability to decipher First Causes, and instead pursues a Comtean synthesis of sensation, fetichistic reasoning, and analysis.15 Comte's version of the evolution of mind and knowledge satisfied the imagina- tion, allowing as it did for the copresence of multiple "moods"—fetichistic and an- alytical—in modern art and consciousness. However, the science of culture's very different accounts of the evolution of the intellect claimed an empirical authority not easily disputed, especially for writers, like Hardy, who were persuaded of the truth of evolution. Throughout The Return of the Native, we encounter commentaries whose cultural oppositions and descriptions of primitive survivals are informed by contemporary anthropological discourse. Juxtaposed with the opening personifica- tions of the heath, for example, are the observations that the somberness of the heath was "distasteful to our race when it was young" (54), but it may "be all of na- ture that is absolutely in keeping with the moods of the more thinking among mankind," because Egdon "appealed to a subtler and scarcer instinct, to a more re- cently learnt emotion" (55). The first specimen of humanity who appears on the scene of the prehistoric heath, Diggory Venn, the reddleman, is identified as "one of a class rapidly becoming extinct in Wessex, filling at present in the rural world the place which, during the last century, the dodo occupied in the world of animals... a curious, interesting, and nearly perished link between obsolete forms of life and those which generally prevail" (59). And Susan Nunsuch's waxen effigy of Eustacia is represented as a "ghastly invention of superstition ... a practice well known on Egdon at that date, and one that is not quite extinct at the present day" (422). Anthropological constructions of relationships between the primitive and the civilized had, furthermore, raised not only epistemological and representational is- sues but social issues as well.16 The "doctrine of survivals" in particular ratified the analogy between alien lower races and domestic lower classes, and it shifted ways of valuing and perceiving the quaint folkways of rural laboring classes. Tylor was cer- tainly a more liberal and sensitive theoretician of primitive culture than many, yet his comparison of the "barbarous hordes with civilized nations" is alert to social dis- tinctions: there is, he observes, "scarce a hand's breadth difference between an Downloaded by [Columbia University] at 12:49 14 November 2014

NARRATING THE NATIVE 155 English ploughman and a negro of central africa" (1: 7). With his "hatchet and hoe," his "food roasting over a log fire" and his tales of "ghosts" (1:7), the European peasant—not the intellectually advanced man—stands in closest proximity to prim- itive man. And it is precisely these outmoded customs and habits of mind (hatchets and superstitions) that Tylor regarded as inimical to the progress of civilization: "It is a harsher, and at times painful, office of ethnography to expose the remains of crude old culture ... and to mark these out for destruction. Yet this work ... is urgently needful for the good of mankind" (2: 453). In The Return of the Native, uneducated, rustic peasants coexist uneasily with edu- cated "modern type[s]" (225), and the narration is equivocal in its judgement of each. The significance and value of the survival of primitive culture among the rus- tic heathfolk are a matter of ambivalence and uncertainty, and I would agree with Bruce Johnson that Hardy never makes up his mind about survivals.17 It is, however, worth pointing out here that social evolutionary theories of survivals themselves contain conceptual contradictions. One of the most difficult cultural evolutionary concepts to formulate was die idea of survivals, precisely because the anthropolo- gists were trying to argue for the perfunctoriness (or functionlessness) of behaviors and beliefs that enjoyed a continuing existence—that, in fact, survived, "carried on by force ofhabit into a new state of society" (Tylor 1:16, my emphasis). In the Origins of Civilisation and Primitive Condition of Man (1870), Sir John Lubbock explains the persistence of savage ideas "passing among ourselves" with tangled analogies: prim- itive ideas, he notes, are "rooted in our minds, as fossils imbedded in the soil" (1). Like a living and vital plant, ideas are "rooted," while at the same time they are, like long-dead fossils, impotently embedded in living material of consciousness. In the volume Studies in Ancient History, John McLennan became similarly entangled in ex- plaining the abstraction: "[W]e can trace everywhere, disguised under a variety of symbolical forms in the higher layer of civilization, the rude modes of life" of prim- itive man (4). "Symbolical" here signifies perfunctoriness, the mere outward show of the civilized customs. Yet the adjective, "disguised," might suggest that the rude modes of primitive man's life are operative in higher layers and are merely masked by the veneer of civilization (an argument that later Victorian feminists, like Mona Caird, would in fact advance to account for the degraded status of women in nine- teenth-century civilized society). The social evolutionists' geological and paleonto- logical metaphors are deployed to highlight the inertness of the traces of the primitive behavior among the civilized. However, their contradictions expose the strain of trying to imagine the behaviors and beliefs of living communities as dead cultural fragments. The Return of the Native's cultural commentary on the indigenous heathfolk and their "not quite extinct" ways is marked with peculiar tensions and dissonances. Consider, for example, the reflections on the Christmas mummers' annual r e - enactment of the St. George legend. The narrator's distinction between revivals and survivals conforms closely to Tylor's characterization of the two cultural phe- nomena. However, the mythologizing of the mysterious grandeur of the natives' Downloaded by [Columbia University] at 12:49 14 November 2014

156 PATRICIA O'HARA "unweeting manner of performance" presents us with a reading and estimation of survivals at odds with anthropological dogma: A traditional pastime is to be distinguished from a mere revival in no more striking feature than in this, that while in the revival all is excitement and fervour, the survival is carried on with a stolidity and ab- sence of stir.... Like Balaam and other unwilling prophets, the agents seem moved by an inner com- pulsion to say and do their allotted parts This unweeting manner of performance is the true ring by which, in this refurbishing age, a fossilized survival may be known from a spurious reproduction. (178) The archaic adjective, "unweeting," indicates "perfunctory" and "unthinking." However, identifying the mechanism of survivals as an "inner compulsion" attrib- utes the persistence of such survivals to a psychic source and the satisfaction of deep-seated human need. Likening the native "agents" to "Balaam and other un- willing prophets" dignifies the "fossilized survival" of Christmas mumming and ele- vates the status of rural folk.18 This way of reading the primitive and its traces in civilized culture runs counter to anthropological thought of the 1870s. Earlier in the novel, the narrator similarly overlaps mythic and evolutionary dis- courses in the ruminations on the "lineal descent [t] " of the annual Guy Fawkes bon- fires from "jumbled Druidical rites": Indeed it is pretty well known that such blazes as this the heathmen were now enjoying are rather the lin- eal descendants from jumbled Druidical rites and Saxon ceremonies than the invention of popular feel- ing about Gunpowder Plot Moreover to light a fire is the instinctive and resistant act of man, when at the winter ingress, the cur- few is sounded throughout nature. It indicates a spontaneous, Promethean rebelliousness against the fiat that this recurrent season shall bring foul times, cold darkness, misery and death. Black chaos comes, and the fettered gods of earth say, Let there be light. (67) The conjuration of an intelligible meaning in this "sky-backed pantomime of sil- houettes" (63) folds Biblical and classical referents into an evolutionarily config- ured lineage of the ancient ritual, elevating the lighting of bonfires to the status of Promethean rebelliousness. Yet it remains a problematic narrative act, insofar as it is the narrator's construction of the significance of the natives' actions, a signifi- cance that is "pretty well known" only among members of an intellectual elite, or "the more thinking among mankind." While the rustics may be agents of unchang- ing human impulses, they are also represented as impediments to progress. The cul- tural space they inhabit is, so to speak, eons away from that of Clym Yeobright and the narrative consciousness that tells his tale. For example, an appreciation of the cosmogonie symbolism of the personified heath, which awaits "last crisis,-the final overthrow" (54), is simply not accessible to the unelevated "clowns," or rustics, who dwell there: In passing from the bucolic to the intellectual life the intermediate stages are usually two at least, fre- quently many more; and one of these stages is almost sure to be worldly advance. We can hardly imag- ine bucolic placidity quickening to intellectual aims without imagining social aims as the transitional phase. Yeobright's local peculiarity was that in striving at high thinking he still cleaved to plain living— nay, wild and meagre living in many respects, and brotherliness with clowns To argue upon the Downloaded by [Columbia University] at 12:49 14 November 2014

NARRATING THE NATIVE 157 possibility of culture before luxury to the bucolic world may be to argue truly, but it is an attempt to dis- turb a sequence to which humanity has been long accustomed. (230-31) This is perhaps the most cynical passage in a novel that, compared to Hardy's later ones, is relatively muted in its depiction of the consequences of the ignorant, grasp- ing "social aims" of the rustic, "bucolic world." The quixotic idealism of Clym's pro- gram for the cultural edification of the natives is underscored by the evolutionary language of the passage, which attributes his inevitable failure to an immutable "evolutionary" sequence that cannot be redirected. Given this "sequence" of the progress of civilization, Clym will never be able to elevate the "clowns" because they aspire to luxury, and not the sweetness and light of "culture." From a distance— cultural and spatial—the natives of Egdon materialize as silhouetted actors in the pantomime of ancient rituals, like the Melstock Quire whose nighttime sojourns "suggested some processional design of Greek or Etruscan pottery" (40). In close proximity, however, they appear more like "clowns," dancing jigs and trading su- perstitions. Do they have access to the primitive modes of perception that the nar- rator seeks to rekindle in his flights of personification? Or are their superstitions and rituals to be understood anthropologically, as ossified survivals of a now defunct cultural past5 The voices of past and present that sound through the narration refuse to settle into a unitary, univocal rendition of "the native." The (self) presentation of rustic characters in mimetic dialogue shows a similar doubleness.19 The heathfolk display in their conversations a resistance to the march of progress, and the comic effect that their commentary generates discredits their views as ignorant and reactionary. This is especially the case with their conversations about learning and literacy: " 'Ah, there's too much of that sending to school in these days!' " complains Captain Vye, " 'It only does harm. Every gatepost and barn door you come to is sure to have some bad word or other chalked upon it by the young rascals: a woman can hardly pass for shame sometimes. If they'd never been taught how to write they wouldn't have been able to scribble such villainy. Their fa- thers couldn't do it, and the country was all the better for it' " (163). Literacy, in other words, brings not the Promethean fires of knowledge, but the graffiti of "young rascals." The claim that "the country was all the better" when folks could not read is ironic to the reader of the text, not to the illiterate auditors of Vye. In a late-nineteenth-century context, the ironic undermining of Vye's view of the edu- cation of native sons coincides with the social evolutionary imperative to elevate the lower levels of contemporary society and thus affirms the reverse of Vye's claim— affirms, that is, that the country would benefit from universal education. The dou- ble—voicing of the dialogue acts to endorse a prevalent way of regarding the peasantry, pointedly expressed by the author of a late-century volume, Annals of the British Peasantry: "The school master ... it is who can bring this inert mass of hu- manity to glow with ambitious fires ... the peasant is still like a child, and treats every fresh gift that he receives as though it were a toy" (Garnier 417). Yet like so many nineteenth-century texts, The Return of the Native charts the gains and losses that attend progress and improvement. 158 PATRICIA O'HARA ing hints that the acquisition of literacy exacts a price from the literate. In response to a discussion of Wildeve, the engineer who has fallen to the low estate of keeping a public house ("his learning was no use to him at all"), Oily the broom maker ob- serves, "And yet how people do strive after [education] and get it! The class of folk that couldn't use to make a round O to save their bones from the pit can write their names now without a sputter of the pen, often-times without a single blot what do I say?—why, almost without a desk to lean their stomachs and elbows upon." "True," replies Humphrey, "tis amazing what a polish the world have been brought to" (73). Humphrey's marvelling at this apex of civilized progress—well-formed letters—is surely parodied here. Yet perhaps the very notion of progress—or "polish" of "the world"—is parodied as well. The discussion continues with Fairway's recollection of how Humphrey's father, like many nonliterate natives, had signed his "X" in the marriage registry: "There stood thy father's cross with arms stretched out like a great banging scarecrow. What a terrible black cross that was—thy father's very like- ness in en!" (74). In diat the marriage of Humphrey's mother and father was a state of disharmony, the scarecrow hanging on the "terrible black cross" can be read as a fully achieved signature, one in which symbol and meaning are joined. Humphrey's father's "X" possesses far more expressive power than the "signing [of] the book" (221) with which the culturally advanced Wildeve and Thomasin seal their most dismal union. Neither the narrator nor the reader, it seems, can ever fully return to that expres- sive past In the "Aftercourses" section of the narrative proper, the reader once more returns to the ancient past of the face on which time makes but little impression: [Clym] frequently walked the heath alone, when the past seized upon him with its shadowy hand, and held him there to listen to its tale. His imagination would then people the spot with its ancient inhabi- tants: forgotten Celtic tribes trod their tracks about him, and he could almost live among them, look in their faces, and see them standing beside the barrows which swelled around.... Those of the dyed bar- barians who had chosen the cultivable tracts were, in comparison with those who had left their marks here, as writers on paper beside writers on parchment... [Y]et they had all lived and died unconscious of the different fates awaiting their relics. It reminded him that unforeseen factors operate in the evolu- tion of immortality. (449) The past has tales to tell. It is the reading of their traces on the paper and parch- ment of culture that is so vexing, so tenuous. The tales are elusive, and the "imagi- nation" cannot be trusted: one can "almost," but not quite, "people" the past Yet the novel questions how completely we can ever leave "the native"—the birthplace of consciousness—in the first place. Like Victorian anthropology, The Return of the Native contemplates the cultural journey from primitive infancy to civilized matu- rity. But where anthropology plotted an upward, progressive "nobler tendency of advancing culture" (Tylor 1:157), which made the past legible and the future pos- sible, The Return of the Native offers no such sureties. Its meditations on the cultural past and present lead only to dislocations—to a condition analogous to that of the returned native, Clym Yeobright, last seen as a man of "less than thirty-three" (474), suffering from a "wrinkled mind" (448).
